sections.html: Pseudotropheus johannii is an mbuna endemic to Lake Malawi, found in shallow rocky coastal areas around Masinje Rocks and Cape Ngombo. Males are blue-black with bright blue striping and females orange. The blacker dominant males separate it from the bluer P. cyaneorhabdos, and it is sometimes sold as 'electric blue johanni'. Less aggressive than most Melanochromis, it can be housed with similarly-sized mbuna. It is still often sold as Melanochromis johanni.

The bluegray mbuna or electric blue johanni (Melanochromis johannii) was imported from Lake Malawi as early as 1972. In the wild, these Aufwuchs-feeding rock cichlids (mbunas) remain about a third smaller than in the aquarium, where they can grow to a maximum length of 12 cm.
Endemic to Lake Malawi. It is found around Masinje Rocks and Cape Ngombo.
It is usually found in relatively shallow water in rocky coastal areas.
Standard length: 12 cm SL. Aquarium base: 90 × 45 cm. Volume: ~154 litres (90 × 45 × 38 cm).

Much of the aquarium should contain piles of rocks arranged to form caves with small areas of open water between. A sandy substrate is best and the water should be well oxygenated. Plants should not be used as they will be eaten.
The water should not be too cool (26-28°C) and the pH should be well above 7.5. Frequent water changes ensure low-pollution water, which is also important.

P. johannii will accept most foods offered but vegetable matter in the form of spirulina flakes, blanched spinach etc. should form a large proportion of the diet. This can be supplemented with live and frozen varieties.
To keep these fish colorful and vital even after hundreds of generations in the aquarium, they must not be fed too fat- and protein-rich food, but need a diet rich in fiber and vitamins.

Quite aggressive but it is not as pronounced in this species as with most other Melanochromis species. It can be housed successfully with similarly-sized mbuna and can even be kept with similarly sized peaceful species such as Aulonocara or Neolamprologus. If it is kept in a mbuna community the tank should be overcrowded to reduce aggression and territory formation. Male fish are aggressive and territorial towards conspecifics and a large tank is required if more than one male is to be kept. Several females should be kept per male.

Because of their aggressiveness, mbunas are best kept in large groups of both sexes: 10 animals are good, 20 better. The aquarium should also have many hiding places where inferior specimens and breeding females can retreat.
This species exhibits very clear sexual dimorphism. Male fish are blue-black with bright blue striping while females are orange in colour. Males also tend to be slightly larger than females.

At about 5 cm in length, the males begin to color. They then get a bright blue base coloration, while the females remain orange. Juveniles show female coloration. However, when a male gets tired of being constantly beaten up by the boss (mbunas are quite aggressive fish), he puts on female clothes and then has peace for the time being. Males disguised as females can always be recognized by the eggspots in the anal fin, which are missing in females.

Relatively easy. Maternal mouthbrooder. It should be spawned in a species tank in a harem of one male and at least 3 females. A 90 cm aquarium is a good size and this should be furnished as suggested above, along with some flat stones and areas of open substrate to act as potential spawning sites. The pH should be around 8.2-8.5 and the temperature 25–26.5 °C. The fish should be conditioned with plenty of live, frozen and vegetable foods.

The male fish will clean and then display around his chosen spawning site, showing intense colour, and attempt to entice females to mate with him. He can be quite aggressive in his pursuits and it is in order to dissipate this aggression that this species should be spawned in a harem. When a female is willing, she will approach the spawning site and lay her eggs there, after which she immediately picks them up in her mouth. The male fish has egg-shaped spots on his anal fin and the female is attracted to these. When she tries to add them to the brood in her mouth she actually receives sperm from the male, thus fertilising the eggs.

The female may carry the eggs for around 3 weeks before releasing the free swimming fry. She will not eat during this period and can be easily spotted by her distended mouth. If a female is overly stressed she may spit out the brood prematurely or eat them, so care must be taken if you decide to move the fish in order to avoid fry predation. It is also worth noting that if a female is away from the colony for too long she may lose her position in the pecking order of the group. It is recommended to wait as long as possible before moving a female unless she is being harassed.

Some breeders artificially strip the fry from the mother's mouth at the 2 week stage and raise them from that point as this usually results in a larger number of fry. The fry are large enough to take brine shrimp nauplii from the time of release. The female will continue to guard the brood for the first week or so following their release, taking them into her mouth when she feels threatened.

M. johannii has been popular since its first importation and is always available as offspring for aquarium enthusiasts all over the world. They are typical agamous mouthbrooders in the female: after spawning the male does not take care of the female and the offspring.

This species can be distinguished from the similar P. cyaneorhabdos by the overall black colouration of dominant males, as opposed to the more blueish patterning of cyaneorhabdos. It is sometimes sold as "electric blue johanni". Do not keep it with other Melanochromis species as they may hybridise.

The generic classification of the mbunas is based to a large extent on the pattern of markings. Melanochromis has horizontal dark bars, and in males the pattern reverses with the onset of sexual maturity: what was previously yellow becomes black, for example, and what was previously black becomes blue, as in the well-known auratus cichlid, M. auratus. Because this does not occur in M. johannii, where the black streaking in males and females remains the same and only the basic coloration changes, it has been suggested to place M. johannii in Pseudotropheus. Some follow the suggestion, others do not. In the end, this is of rather minor importance in aquaristics.
